QF.id: IV Strategies Using Interest Rate Derivatives_75

question.text: A pension fund holds long-duration government bonds and has sold covered calls to generate extra income. Interest rates have fallen sharply and bond prices have risen above the call strike. What should the fund manager consider?

answer.text: The fund's upside above the call strike is capped/offset by the short call, so the manager should reassess the position and square off or adjust the option if the market view changes
No action needed since covered calls always maximize returns
The fund should immediately sell all bonds to lock in gains
The manager should buy more calls to increase upside potential

explanation.text: The Logic: A covered call generates extra income but caps the upside near the sold-call strike. With bond prices above the strike, the short call offsets further gains. Exchange-traded interest rate options are cash-settled, so there is no physical delivery — the manager's choice is whether to keep the capped position, square off, or adjust the option to reflect the new view. The Trap: Covered calls do not always maximize returns; they trade upside for premium. Selling all the bonds outright is a different decision driven by portfolio policy, not by the option being in the money. Buying more calls is a separate, directional strategy. Note: Once a covered call is deep in the money, the income from the premium is effectively earned, but further upside is locked out. Treat any adjustment as a fresh decision based on the current market view, not as a reflex.
